claims.text: Inducing a nanocrystalline microstructure in refractory high-entropy alloys can increase yield strength and ductility while maintaining high-temperature and irradiation stability.
WTaCrVHf is a quinary nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy investigated for extreme irradiation environments.
Severe plastic deformation can produce the proposed nanocrystalline refractory-HEA microstructure.
Optimized additive manufacturing or post-processing can produce the proposed nanocrystalline refractory-HEA microstructure.
Nanocrystalline structures have a higher density of grain boundaries than coarse-grained structures.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries act as effective sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries promote dislocation motion.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries restrict dislocation movement and thereby increase yield strength.
Grain boundaries provide defect-annihilation sites that preserve thermal and irradiation stability.
Nanometre-grained refractory-HEA pillars can reach yield strengths of approximately 10 GPa, about one order of magnitude above their bulk form.
Nanocrystalline refractory HEAs can show compressive plastic strains over 30%.
Compressive ductility improves by over 30% relative to a coarse-grained baseline.
Nanocrystalline WTaCrVHf exhibits low irradiation-defect generation and evolution under dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation.
Nanocrystalline WTaCrVHf shows no detectable grain growth under the reported extreme irradiation exposures.
Nanometre-grained refractory-HEA films remain stable after exposure at 1100 °C for three days.
The simultaneous strength, ductility, thermal-stability, and irradiation-stability benefits will hold in a single refractory-HEA system at 900–1100 °C under helium or heavy-ion irradiation.
Grain sizes below 10 nm may cause grain-boundary-related embrittlement.
Processing-induced secondary phases could offset the mechanical and stability benefits of grain refinement.

contradictions.description: The structural-mediator field says grain boundaries promote dislocation motion, whereas the mechanism field says they restrict dislocation movement. These opposite descriptions are not reconciled.
